name: DEXA body fat scan
summary: A low-dose X-ray scan that splits the body into fat, lean and bone, and the reference most forum members use to check their body fat number.
lead: Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA or DXA) is an imaging test that passes X-rays at two energy levels through the body and uses the difference in absorption to separate bone from soft tissue. It is the most widely used technology for measuring bone mineral density and is chiefly used to diagnose and monitor osteopenia and osteoporosis . The same scan can also report whole-body and regional fat mass and lean mass, which is the use that appears in looksmaxxing discussions.
claims: A DEXA scan is the way to confirm your real body-fat percentage.

name: Gastric bypass (Roux-en-Y)
summary: Major bariatric surgery that reroutes the gut for large, sustained weight loss, aimed at medical obesity rather than cosmetic leaning.
lead: Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB) is a bariatric operation in which the stomach is divided into a small upper pouch, typically about 15 to 30 mL, and a larger remnant; the small intestine is then rearranged into a Y so that food bypasses most of the stomach and the duodenum . It is performed for severe obesity and its complications, and it is one of the best-studied weight-loss operations.

name: Gastric balloon / endoscopic sleeve
summary: Non-surgical stomach-reduction devices and stitching procedures that produce modest to moderate weight loss, with real procedural risks.
lead: An intragastric balloon (gastric balloon) is an inflatable device placed in the stomach to help with weight loss when diet and exercise have not worked and surgery is not wanted or recommended. It takes up space in the stomach, which causes earlier fullness and slower gastric emptying . Devices are usually filled with saline, and some contain a dye that colors urine if the balloon leaks .

name: CoolSculpting (cryolipolysis)
summary: Controlled cold applied to a patch of fat to reduce it without surgery; studies show modest local reductions and a rare paradoxical-growth risk.
lead: Cryolipolysis, often called fat freezing, is a non-invasive procedure that uses controlled cooling of subcutaneous fat for localized fat reduction. The term is frequently used interchangeably with the brand name CoolSculpting, introduced in the United States in 2010 by Zeltiq Aesthetics and acquired by Allergan Aesthetics in 2017 . The FDA has cleared it for several body areas including the submental area, jawline, arms, flanks, abdomen and thighs .
claims: Freezing fat is a legitimate way to get local fat loss, even from the face.
Cold causes white fat to convert to brown fat that burns off.

name: Ultrasound cavitation / body contouring
summary: Low-frequency ultrasound devices marketed for fat reduction, used at home by some forum members; no published results in the sources show cosmetic outcomes.
lead: Ultrasonic cavitation, as used in cosmetic body contouring, refers to devices that deliver low-frequency ultrasound to the skin with the aim of reducing localized subcutaneous fat. In physics, cavitation is the formation and collapse of vapor-filled bubbles in a liquid when the local pressure falls below the liquid's vapor pressure, and it can produce shock waves and high local temperatures . Cosmetic proponents apply the term to ultrasound-induced bubbles in fatty tissue.
claims: Ultrasonic cavitation can spot-reduce facial fat at home.
It permanently destroys fat cells non-invasively, and is a hardmaxx option for already lean people.
The method has real risks if misused.

name: EMSculpt muscle stimulation
summary: A clinic device that triggers intense muscle contractions with focused electromagnetic energy to tone muscle and, with the Neo version, add heat to reduce fat.
lead: EMSCULPT (BTL Industries) is a non-invasive body-contouring treatment that uses high-intensity focused electromagnetic (HIFEM) energy to stimulate muscle contractions in areas such as the abdomen and buttocks. A 2024 systematic review describes EMSCULPT NEO as an FDA-cleared treatment for increasing muscle tone and reducing fat, in which HIFEM builds muscle mass and combined radiofrequency is intended to reduce fat .

name: Lipodissolve (phosphatidylcholine injections)
summary: Unapproved fat-dissolving injections of phosphatidylcholine and deoxycholate; small uncontrolled reports of fat reduction, no approved product, and documented infections and inflammation.
lead: Lipodissolve, also known as injection lipolysis or PC/DC injection, is a cosmetic procedure in which a mixture of phosphatidylcholine (PC) and sodium deoxycholate (DC) is injected into subcutaneous fat with the aim of reducing small localized deposits. It belongs to the broader family of mesotherapy techniques, in which substances are injected into or just beneath the skin.
claims: Lipodissolve melts localized fat without surgery
Phosphatidylcholine is the active fat-dissolving ingredient
Compounded injections are as safe as approved products

name: Body fat calipers
summary: Pinch-style skinfold calipers estimate body fat from fold thickness; cheap and good for tracking your own changes, less reliable as an absolute percentage.
lead: Body fat calipers, also called skinfold calipers or plicometers, are hand-held instruments that measure the thickness of a pinched fold of skin and the fat beneath it at standardized body sites. The readings are used in equations that estimate whole-body fat percentage. The method is also known as the pinch test.
claims: Calipers give a cheap, accurate body fat percentage at home
Calipers are best for tracking change over time

name: Body wraps
summary: Spa wraps and sauna suits marketed for slimming; the temporary inch loss is water, per the FDA.
lead: Body wraps are cosmetic or spa treatments in which part of the body is wrapped in bandages, plastic film or neoprene, often after application of mud, herbal preparations or lotions, and sometimes combined with a PVC sauna suit. Wikipedia's article on mud wraps notes that body wraps redirect to it.
claims: Wraps shrink inches overnight
Wraps remove toxins
Wraps are harmless

name: Peg-MGF (mechano growth factor)
summary: A pegylated synthetic version of the IGF-1Ec peptide sold as a research chemical for muscle growth; human evidence is absent and it is WADA-banned.
lead: Mechano growth factor (MGF), also called IGF-1Ec, is a naturally occurring 24-amino-acid peptide produced from the IGF-1 gene during muscle repair after exercise, and is described as having anabolic effects. PEG-MGF is a pegylated synthetic form sold as a research chemical.
claims: Peg-MGF triggers muscle growth after training
Pegylation makes MGF active long enough to work

name: Insulin (bodybuilding use)
summary: Prescription diabetes hormone injected by some bodybuilders for muscle fullness; evidence for benefit is thin and hypoglycemia has been linked to deaths.
lead: Insulin is a peptide hormone that regulates blood glucose and is the main anabolic hormone of the body: it helps muscle and fat take in glucose, increases amino-acid uptake and protein synthesis, and slows liver glucose production and breakdown of fat and protein. As a medicine it is used for diabetes.
claims: Insulin drives nutrients into muscle for faster growth
Insulin use can be managed safely

name: Prohormones (1-Andro, 4-AD)
summary: Steroid precursors once sold as supplements; androstenedione was banned in the US in 2004 and studies found little muscle benefit.
lead: Prohormones are precursor compounds converted in the body to active hormones. In bodybuilding supplement culture the term covers androstenedione (4-AD, or andro) and related compounds such as 1-androstenedione, which were sold over the counter as testosterone boosters before regulatory action.
claims: Andro raises testosterone and builds muscle
Prohormones are a safe legal alternative to steroids

name: Casein protein
summary: Slow-digesting milk protein taken before bed; digestion is well documented, appearance benefit untested.
lead: Casein is the main protein family in milk, making up roughly 80% of cow's milk protein, and is sold as a powdered supplement (commonly micellar casein or calcium caseinate) in the bodybuilding and fitness market . In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed mainly as a slow-digesting protein taken before bed to support muscle mass.
claims: Casein before bed reduces muscle breakdown overnight
Casein raises IGF-1 more than whey
Whey only after training, casein the rest of the time

name: Laxogenin
summary: Plant steroid-like saponin sold for muscle; research is lab and plant work only, no human trials.
lead: Laxogenin is a plant-derived steroidal sapogenin (3-beta-hydroxy-5-alpha-spirostan-6-one) first characterised from plants such as Allium chinense (the 'Xiebai' bulb of Chinese medicine) and Smilax sieboldii . It is sold in bodybuilding supplements under claims of muscle-building, often described as a 'plant steroid'.

name: Tribulus terrestris
summary: Herbal 'testosterone booster' sold since the 1980s; controlled studies have not consistently shown a hormone effect.
lead: Tribulus terrestris (puncture vine, goathead) is a spiny annual plant of the caltrop family, native to warm regions of Eurasia and Africa and invasive elsewhere . Its fruit and leaf extracts have been used in traditional Chinese and Ayurvedic medicine and have been sold since the 1980s as a supplement intended to raise testosterone for bodybuilding or sexual function .

name: Caffeine pre-workout
summary: Stimulant-based training powders; caffeine is the best-supported ingredient and the rest is mixed.
lead: Pre-workout supplements are multi-ingredient powders, capsules or drinks taken before training to increase energy, focus and endurance; caffeine is their near-universal base, found in 86% of bestselling products in one analysis . Other typical ingredients include creatine, beta-alanine, citrulline, amino acids and nitrates .

name: Essential amino acids (EAAs)
summary: The nine dietary amino acids as a powder; they drive muscle protein synthesis, but aesthetic payoff versus ordinary protein is unstudied.
lead: Essential amino acids (EAAs) are nine amino acids that humans cannot synthesise fast enough to meet needs and must obtain from food: histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan and valine . EAA supplements sell these as a free-form powder, positioned in fitness communities as an alternative to protein powder for muscle building, especially during dieting.

name: Epicatechin
summary: Cocoa/tea flavanol marketed as a myostatin inhibitor; evidence is small muscular-dystrophy pilots, not lifters.
lead: (-)-Epicatechin is a flavan-3-ol, a type of plant polyphenol found in cocoa, green tea, apples and berries . As a supplement it is promoted for muscle growth on the theory that it lowers myostatin and raises follistatin.

name: Phosphatidic acid
summary: A membrane lipid sold as a pre-workout supplement because it signals to mTOR in cells; direct human evidence for added muscle is small and thin.
lead: Phosphatidic acid (PA) is the simplest glycerophospholipid: a glycerol backbone carrying two fatty acid chains and a phosphate group. It is a precursor for other membrane lipids and also acts as a signaling molecule inside cells .
claims: Taking PA around training activates mTOR and adds extra muscle.

name: Mass gainer powders
summary: Calorie-dense carb-and-protein shake powders for lifters who struggle to eat enough; they add calories, and the evidence is about overall energy intake rather than the powder itself.
lead: A mass gainer, or weight gainer, is a high-calorie powder supplement designed to help people gain weight and muscle by supplying a large amount of energy, mostly from carbohydrate with moderate protein and some fat, in a drinkable form .
claims: Mass gainers harm gut health and may cause acne, so whole food is better.
Carbs and calories matter more than large amounts of protein for gaining.

name: Site enhancement oil (Synthol)
summary: Oil injected straight into muscle to make it look bigger; case reports document embolism, granulomas, nerve damage and infection.
lead: Site enhancement oil (SEO), often called Synthol, santol or by the practice name "fluffing," is oil injected into muscle to increase its size or change its shape .

name: Progressive overload hypertrophy training
summary: The principle of steadily increasing load, reps or volume to keep muscles adapting; widely taught in strength science, with the details of how best to progress still debated.
lead: Progressive overload is a training principle in which the stress placed on the musculoskeletal and nervous systems is gradually increased so that strength and muscle mass continue to develop .

name: Push/pull/legs (PPL)
summary: A three-way weekly training split (pushing muscles, pulling muscles, legs); popular in lifting circles, and no cited research ranks it above other splits.
lead: Push/pull/legs (PPL) is a training split that divides weekly resistance training into push, pull and leg days. Wikipedia defines a split as how a trainee divides weekly training volume across muscle groups and days, and lists push/pull/legs among common splits .

name: Bro split
summary: A weekly routine that trains one muscle group per day; widely used in bodybuilding culture, with no cited research ranking it against other splits.
lead: The bro split is a weekly training split in which different muscle groups are trained on separate days, typically one group per session. Wikipedia names it as one of the common splits, along with full body, upper/lower and push/pull/legs .

name: Beginner strength programs (5x5, SS, GZCLP)
summary: Linear-progression barbell routines that beginners use to add size and strength, with plenty of coaching lore and no head-to-head trials.
lead: Beginner strength programs are structured barbell routines built around a few compound lifts, such as the squat, bench press, overhead press and deadlift, in which the load is increased by a small fixed amount at each session or week. This approach is usually called linear progression. Three names are most often used in lifting communities: 5x5 (five sets of five repetitions, including the StrongLifts variant), Starting Strength (often abbreviated SS, from Mark Rippetoe's book), and GZCLP (a tiered linear-progression template shared online).
claims: A simple linear progression program is the fastest way for a novice to get bigger and stronger.
Heavy compound lifts build a better-proportioned physique than machine or isolation work.

name: High intensity training (HIT / Mentzer)
summary: Mentzer's Heavy Duty: one or few sets to failure with long rests, famous in bodybuilding history, untested as a complete system.
lead: High-intensity training (HIT) is a strength-training method centred on brief, infrequent workouts in which each set is taken to momentary muscular failure. It was popularised in the 1970s by Arthur Jones, founder of Nautilus . Mike Mentzer, an American professional bodybuilder, later developed his own version called Heavy Duty, which used very few sets and long recovery periods .
claims: One set to failure, with long rest between sessions, builds muscle as well as or better than many sets.
Training only once every 4-7 days is optimal.

name: Renaissance Periodization (RP) volume training
summary: Israetel's MEV/MAV/MRV set-count framework: popular in lifting circles, with no independent trial of the system itself.
lead: Renaissance Periodization (RP) is a fitness company co-founded in 2012 by Mike Israetel and Nick Shaw . It is associated with a volume-management framework for muscle building built around three weekly set benchmarks: minimum effective volume (MEV), maximum adaptive volume (MAV) and maximum recoverable volume (MRV) .
claims: Each muscle has a personal range of weekly sets (MEV to MRV) that should guide programming.

name: Blood flow restriction (BFR) training
summary: Cuff-assisted light-load lifting with a real rehab research base; the height-growth versions on forums have no study behind them.
lead: Blood flow restriction (BFR) training is a method in which a cuff or band placed on the upper arm or thigh partly restricts blood flow while a person exercises with light loads. It was developed by Dr. Yoshiaki Sato in Japan in 1966, where it is known as KAATSU .
claims: Restricting blood flow during jump rope plus decompression can add 2-4 inches of height.
Light-load BFR builds muscle comparably to heavy lifting.

name: Lengthened partials / stretch training
summary: Overloading only the stretched part of a rep; plausible in hypertrophy theory, thinly documented here.
lead: Lengthened partials are repetitions performed only through the stretched portion of an exercise's range of motion, for example the bottom half of a curl or fly, rather than the full range. They are discussed in lifting communities as a way to emphasise the position in which the muscle is most elongated.

name: Myo-reps / drop sets
summary: Time-saving to-failure set techniques; drop sets have a long history, myo-reps are newer and only just trialled.
lead: Drop sets and myo-reps are resistance-training intensity techniques meant to pack more hard repetitions into less time. A drop set continues exercising with a lighter weight after reaching muscle failure at a heavier one . Myo-reps are a related method in which a lifter performs an initial high-effort set and then several short mini-sets with brief rests; a 2026 trial compared the approach with traditional straight sets in resistance-trained men .
claims: Myo-reps give the same muscle growth as straight sets in less time.
Drop sets build more muscle than conventional sets.
